claims: El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon.
El Niño is marked by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central/eastern equatorial Pacific.
El Niño involves weakening trade winds.
El Niño triggers global weather shifts.
El Niño occurs every 2–7 years.
El Niño often causes flooding in South America.
El Niño often causes droughts in Australia.
El Niño often causes droughts in Indonesia.
El Niño often causes warmer, wetter winters in the Southern U.S.
El Niño causes increased winter precipitation in the South U.S. and California.
During El Niño, the North U.S. and Pacific Northwest tend to be warmer and drier.
During El Niño, parts of the Amazon often experience droughts and severe fire risk.
El Niño generally reduces hurricane activity in the Atlantic Basin due to higher wind shear.
El Niño increases hurricane activity in the Pacific.
During El Niño, there is a reduction in nutrient-rich cold water upwelling along the South American coast.
The reduction in nutrient-rich cold water upwelling along the South American coast severely impacts fishing.
The reduction in nutrient-rich cold water upwelling along the South American coast reduces fish populations.
The reduction in nutrient-rich cold water upwelling along the South American coast causes coral bleaching.
El Niño occurs when easterly trade winds weaken or reverse.
Easterly trade winds weakening or reversing allows warm ocean water built up in the west to move east towards South America.
NOAA monitors El Niño using satellite data.
NOAA monitors El Niño using ocean buoys.
NOAA monitors El Niño using sea level pressure measurements in the Niño-3.4 region.
El Niño events typically last for 9–12 months.
El Niño events usually begin in the summer.
El Niño events usually peak in the winter.
A Super El Niño occurs when Pacific water temperatures exceed 2°C above average.
Super El Niño causes more intense, extreme, and widespread global impacts.
